newsitem.title: UK: Bruton challenges IRA to call N.Irish truce.
newsitem.headline: Bruton challenges IRA to call N.Irish truce.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton urged IRA guerrillas on Tuesday to call an immediate truce and put Northern Ireland's shattered peace process back on track.

Ahead of talks with President Bill Clinton in Washington, Bruton played down Anglo-Irish differences on rebuilding the region's peace momentum, and said they key lay with the outlawed Irish Republican Army, which is fighting British rule.
"I believe that (an IRA ceasefire) is the main priority now," Bruton said in a BBC radio interview in the United States capital which was broadcast in Northern Ireland.

"Basically what we are looking for from the Republican movement is, in a sense, a declaration of self-confidence...in their own ability to negotiate freely with others, using their intellectual talents and their political skills without recourse to violence."

The IRA abandoned a 17-month truce last February accusing Britain of refusing it a voice in all-party political talks on the future of Northern Ireland where the 60 per cent Protestant majority support rule from London.

Irish nationalist politicians' hopes for a new truce received a setback recently when British Prime Minister John Major rejected proposals from Catholic moderate leader John Hume aimed at speeding access to talks by the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm.

London and Dublin are agreed that the IRA must declare a ceasefire before Sinn Fein is given a place in talks but a meeting between Bruton and Major earlier this month failed to bridge a gap on the timing of Sinn Fein's entry.
Major says his intelligence agencies must determine whether any new IRA cessation is genuine and intended to last, unlike the first which Britain says was a short-term tactic.
Ireland is opposed to a lengthy delay in bringing Sinn Fein to the talks table once it has subscribed to principles of non-violence and an IRA truce is deemed to be credible.
Bruton was due to meet Clinton at the White House around 9.45 a.m. (1445 GMT) on Tuesday to review the Northern Irish peace process, officials in Dublin said.
In his radio interview, Bruton stressed progress he had made with Major.

"Look at what we have agreed on. I would say to everybody who is concerned about this (to) look at what's there. Don't be asking about the one-eight that we haven't got, look at the seven-eights that we do have, and say to the IRA call a ceasefire now."
Major denies Sinn Fein charges of stalling its entry to talks and says guerrilla violence is the hurdle.

Sinn Fein demands an unconditional place in talks and says Major is isolating it to buy vital parliamentary support from Protestant Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) legislators for his minority government.
UUP legislators abstained in an important vote on Monday, helping Major stave off a threat of an embarrassing defeat on fisheries policy. They deny any voting deal with Major.
